## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

\# start out with a number to test
x \<- 3
# you'll want your function to return this number
x\^2
square \<- **function**(...) {
...
}
# test it out
square(x)
square(53)
53\^2 \# does this match?

Creating a square function

```{r}
# define x first, save new name for the x^2, then return the new value
x <- 3
square <- function(x) {
	square1 <- x ^ 2
	return(square1)
}

#calling this out to 
square(x)
square(53)
53^2
```

1.  Write a function to raise to any power. You don’t just want to square numbers, you want to raise them to higher powers too. Make a function that uses two arguments, `x` for a number, and `power` for the power. Call it `raise()`.

```{r}

raise <- function(x, power) {
	raise_val <- x^power
	return (raise_val)
}

# test with
raise(x = 6, power = 2)
# should give you
6^2
```

2.  Change your `raise()` function to default to squaring `x` when the user doesn’t enter a value for `power`.

```{r}
#to make the power default include the number you want equal to the power
raise <- function(x, power = 2) {
	raise_val <- x^power
	return (raise_val)
}
#same
raise (x = 3, power = 3)
raise (power = 3, x = 3)

#diff
raise(2,4)
raise(4,2)

# test
raise(x = 5)
# should give you
5^2
```

1.  Create a function that takes a vector of numbers and returns the standard deviation manually (like we did the mean). Use `if` statements to check if the vector has only one (or fewer) elements and return `NA` if so. (Hint: the `length()` function will be helpful!) You don’t need any extra arguments besides the vector of numbers.

sd⁡(𝑥)=√∑𝑛𝑖=1(𝑥𝑖−¯𝑥)2𝑛−1

```{r}

new_sd <- function(x) {
	demeaned_x <- x - mean(x)
	squared_demeaned_x <-demeaned_x^2
	sum_of_squares <- sum(squared_demeaned_x)
	n_minus_1 <- length(x) - 1
	std_dev <- sqrt(sum_of_squares / n_minus_1)
		if (length(x) <= 1) {
			return(NA)
		} else {
		return(std_dev)
		}
}
new_sd(c(345,123,7564,345,123,4653,4346, 346, 76))
sd(c(123, 6564, 345, 123, 4653, 4346, 346, 76))

x<- c(5, 9)

new_sd(x)
sd(x)
```

2.  Modify your function to remove the NA values before calculating the standard deviation. (Hint: the `na.omit()` function will be helpful!) Add an argument `na.rm =` that defaults to `TRUE` (the *opposite* of the `na.rm` argument in the built-in R function `sd()`, which defaults to `FALSE`). If `na.rm = FALSE`, then the function should return `NA` if there are any NA values in the vector.

```{r}

x <- (c(3, 6, 9 , 10))

new_sd <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE) {
	if (na.rm) {
		#remove NAs
		new_x <- na.omit(x)
	} else {
		# done remove NAs
		new_x <- x
	} #will have a new value of x if NAs are removed, same value it not
	
	if (length(new_x) <= 1) {
		return_val <- NA
	} else{
	#ncalculate the std dev using the new x 
		demeaned_x <- new_x - mean(new_x)
		squared_demeaned_x <-demeaned_x^2
		sum_of_squares <- sum(squared_demeaned_x)
		n_minus_1 <- length(new_x) - 1
		return_val <- sqrt(sum_of_squares / n_minus_1)
	}
	return (return_val)
}

new_sd(nlsy$income)
new_sd(c(1))
new_sd(c(1, NA, NA))
new_sd(c(1, 344,556,664,2,4,6,4))
new_sd(c(1, NA, 344,556,NA,664,2,4,6,4))
new_sd(c(1, NA, 3,56,666,4323,NA,3))
```
